title: Willingness-to-pay: why Love beats Utility and Coercion as a durable growth and pricing strategy
summary: Jason Cohen splits willingness-to-pay into three sources: Love, Utility and Coercion. Each one changes growth, retention and exposure to competitors in a different way. His conclusion is that even a cold-blooded investor should build WTP through Love and Utility, and treat Coercion as the weakest base.

principles.text: Create value for the customer first, then decide how to split it: leave surplus for advocacy and retention, or raise prices.
principles.quote: Creating value for the customer comes first. Then--and only then--you can decide how to "split it with the customer," either leveraging Consumer Surplus for advocacy, high-retention, and growth, or indeed by raising prices.

principles.text: Love-based WTP produces cheap, non-linear growth, because happy customers repeat-buy and advocate with no extra sales cost.
principles.quote: **Love** creates *inexpensive, non-linear growth*, because your customers are your allies.

principles.text: Customers who love you stay when a better or cheaper competitor shows up, so Love works as retention and defense against rivals.
principles.quote: When a new competitor arrives, *even when it is superior* in features or price, your customers will stay, because they're here for more than just the features and the price.

principles.text: Utility WTP grows revenue inside existing accounts but does not create advocates and does not stop customers evaluating new competitors.
principles.quote: But, a customer's willingness to buy another ten seats of JIRA doesn't imply the customer is going on forums, spending personal credibility to advocate on your behalf.

principles.text: Coercion (lock-in, monopoly, policy mandates) turns customers into allies of your competitors and leaves you open to disruption by mediocre rivals.
principles.quote: You are constantly vulnerable to disruption, even by mediocre competition. This is the weakest position you could be in, because you're coercing customers instead of delighting them.

principles.text: With identical revenue and profit, the Love-based company is the better bet. Love can add Utility later, but Coercion rarely converts into Love.
principles.quote: It is also possible for (1) to add Utility or even Coercive WTP to their strategy, further strengthening their position, whereas it is much more difficult for (2) to generate Love starting from their current position.
